desc: THE MISSING SPINE. Every incident in this cluster happened inside Strategic Air Command, and until now the board had United States Air Force above and nothing between it and the bases. SAC owned Loring, Wurtsmith, Malmstrom, Minot, Grand Forks, F. E. Warren, Ellsworth and Walker; it ran the alert postures the 1975 documents invoke; and it is SAC command posts that appear as the reporting node in almost every primary record opened for this pass. The 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log for November 1975 reads almost entirely as a record of calls from 'SAC CP' and the 341st Strategic Air Command Post. The National Military Command Center's Loring memorandum of 29 October 1975 records that NORAD was informed of the incident by SAC and that the SAC Command Center reported back on the failure of the Army National Guard helicopter to locate the intruder, citing SAC CP OPS CONTROL 291954Z OCT 75. When Echo Flight went off alert at Malmstrom on 16 March 1967 it was SAC Headquarters that called in Ogden Air Materiel Area support for a complete engineering analysis within hours. The node exists so that a reader can see that these are not scattered base-level anomalies but a run of reports moving up one chain of command, and so that the base hubs have something to attach to.

claims.text: THE PROVENANCE RATIO THAT MAKES THIS CLUSTER DIFFERENT. Of 47 named witnesses in the nuclear register, 26 reached the record through contemporaneous official paper and 13 through a researcher's interview programme. A missile field generates paperwork by design, which is why this seam is documented where most of this subject is only attested.

dossier.narrative:
The reason this node matters more than an organisational chart entry is that it changes what kind of evidence the nuclear cluster rests on.

Of the 47 named witnesses in this cluster's register, 26 reached the record through contemporaneous official paper: message traffic, memoranda for record, duty logs, AF Form 117s and a Blue Book phone log. Thirteen reached it through a researcher's interview programme. That ratio is unusual in this subject and it is entirely a consequence of where these events happened. A missile field generates paperwork by design. A man who sees something in a field does not.

So SAC sits at the centre of the map here as the entity whose routine record-keeping is the evidence. Its bases are the hubs, the incidents attach to the bases, and the witnesses attach to the incidents. Reading outward from this node is reading the chain by which a claim became a document.

What this node does not assert is any conclusion about the objects. The records establish that intrusions were reported, escalated, logged and in several cases responded to with intercepts and alert postures. They do not establish what was intruding, and several of them record that nobody determined it.

dossier.whatItIs: Strategic Air Command, the USAF major command that held the American land-based nuclear deterrent from 1946 to 1992. It owned every installation in this cluster: Malmstrom, Minot, Loring, Wurtsmith, F. E. Warren, Grand Forks and Ellsworth. It is on this map because it is the reporting node in the primary records, not because anyone claims anything about it.
dossier.whyImplicated: It is the institutional spine of the strongest documentary seam this board carries. Where almost everything else in this subject reaches the record through someone's testimony, the nuclear-incursion record reaches it through SAC's own message traffic, duty logs and unit histories. The National Military Command Center's Memorandum for Record of 29 October 1975 states plainly that NORAD was informed of the incident by SAC. The 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log for 7 to 19 November 1975 is in substance a record of calls from SAC posts. When the Echo Flight shutdown happened on 16 March 1967, SAC Headquarters was called within hours and the wing history says so. Whatever one concludes about what was seen, the paper trail is the command's own.
